questions.q: What are the three basic processes of urine formation?
options: Glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion
questions.explain: Excretion = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

open.q: What are the three basic processes of urine formation?

questions.q: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate?
questions.explain: About 180 L of filtrate forms daily, but only about 1.5 L leaves as urine.

open.q: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate?

questions.q: Which pressure is the main force favouring glomerular filtration?
questions.explain: Glomerular capillary pressure of about 60 mmHg pushes fluid out. Capsular pressure and plasma oncotic pressure oppose it.

open.q: Which pressure is the main force favouring glomerular filtration?

questions.q: What is the net filtration pressure if glomerular hydrostatic pressure is 60 mmHg, capsular pressure 18 mmHg and plasma colloid osmotic pressure 32 mmHg?
questions.explain: Net filtration pressure = 60 − (18 + 32) = 10 mmHg.

open.q: What is the net filtration pressure if glomerular hydrostatic pressure is 60 mmHg, capsular pressure 18 mmHg and plasma colloid osmotic pressure 32 mmHg?

questions.q: Which substance, freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, is the standard marker for measuring GFR?
questions.explain: Inulin clearance equals GFR. Creatinine is used clinically instead because it needs no infusion.

open.q: Which substance, freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, is the standard marker for measuring GFR?

questions.q: Which endogenous substance is most used clinically to estimate GFR?
questions.explain: Creatinine is produced steadily by muscle and is filtered with only a little tubular secretion.

open.q: Which endogenous substance is most used clinically to estimate GFR?

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of filtered water and sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule?
questions.explain: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of the filtrate, isotonically.

open.q: Roughly what fraction of filtered water and sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule?

questions.q: By what mechanism is glucose reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
options: Primary active transport by an ATPase
questions.explain: Na⁺ moves down its gradient (set by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase) and carries glucose with it.

open.q: By what mechanism is glucose reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?

questions.q: What is the renal threshold for glucose in plasma?
questions.explain: Above this, the transporters saturate and glucose appears in the urine.

open.q: What is the renal threshold for glucose in plasma?

questions.q: Where does aldosterone mainly act in the nephron?
options: Principal cells of late distal tubule and collecting duct
questions.explain: It increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion there.

open.q: Where does aldosterone mainly act in the nephron?

questions.q: How does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
questions.explain: V2 receptor activation raises cAMP and moves aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane.

open.q: How does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting duct?

questions.q: Which hormone decreases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and promotes natriuresis?
questions.explain: ANP is released when the atria are stretched by volume expansion.

open.q: Which hormone decreases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and promotes natriuresis?

questions.q: Name a substance secreted by the renal tubules.
questions.explain: Tubules secrete H⁺, K⁺, ammonia, creatinine, PAH and many drugs.

open.q: Name a substance secreted by the renal tubules.
open.a: Hydrogen ions (also K⁺, NH₃, creatinine, PAH and many drugs)

questions.q: Clearance of a substance is calculated as:
options: (Urine concentration × urine flow rate) ÷ plasma concentration
(Plasma concentration × urine flow rate) ÷ urine concentration
questions.explain: C = U × V ÷ P. It is the plasma volume cleared of the substance per minute.

open.q: Clearance of a substance is calculated as:

questions.q: How does glomerular filtrate differ from plasma?
options: It has essentially no cells and almost no protein
It contains no glucose or amino acids
It contains no electrolytes, only water
It contains twice as much sodium as plasma
questions.explain: Filtrate is plasma minus its proteins. It contains water, electrolytes, glucose and amino acids, but no red cells and only a negligible amount of protein.

open.q: How does glomerular filtrate differ from plasma?

questions.q: What are the usual normal GFR values for young adult men and women?
options: About 125 mL/min in men and about 90 to 120 mL/min in women
About 125 mL/min in women and about 90 to 120 mL/min in men
About 12.5 mL/min in both men and women
About 1,250 mL/min in men and about 900 mL/min in women
questions.explain: GFR is higher in men because of larger body size and muscle mass. It also depends on age and body size.

open.q: What are the usual normal GFR values for young adult men and women?

questions.q: How does GFR change with age after about 40 years?
questions.explain: GFR declines by roughly 0.4 to 1.2 mL/min each year after 40, so older people have a lower reserve. A GFR that is low for age points to kidney disease.

open.q: How does GFR change with age after about 40 years?

questions.q: What is the filtered load of a substance?
options: Urine flow multiplied by its urine concentration
Its plasma concentration divided by GFR
GFR multiplied by its plasma concentration
questions.explain: Filtered load is the amount of a substance filtered per minute. Excretion = filtered load + secretion - reabsorption.

open.q: What is the filtered load of a substance?

questions.q: What happens to GFR if a ureter is blocked, for example by a stone?
options: It rises as plasma oncotic pressure falls
It falls as Bowman's capsule pressure rises
It rises as Bowman's capsule pressure falls
questions.explain: Back-pressure raises capsular hydrostatic pressure, which opposes filtration. This is a postrenal cause of reduced GFR.

open.q: What happens to GFR if a ureter is blocked, for example by a stone?

questions.q: What is the effect of low plasma protein (hypoproteinaemia) on GFR?
options: GFR rises, because plasma oncotic pressure falls
GFR falls, because the membrane becomes impermeable
GFR falls, because filtration pressure falls
questions.explain: Plasma proteins pull fluid back into the capillary. When they are low, the net filtration pressure rises. Dehydration, which concentrates the proteins, has the opposite effect.

open.q: What is the effect of low plasma protein (hypoproteinaemia) on GFR?

questions.q: What is the immediate effect of mild constriction of the efferent arteriole on glomerular filtration?
options: Glomerular pressure falls and GFR falls
Glomerular pressure rises and GFR rises
questions.explain: Narrowing the outflow raises pressure inside the glomerulus. This is why drugs that dilate the efferent arteriole, such as ACE inhibitors, can lower GFR.

open.q: What is the immediate effect of mild constriction of the efferent arteriole on glomerular filtration?

questions.q: A fall in NaCl delivery to the macula densa leads to which response?
options: Afferent dilation and renin release help restore GFR
questions.explain: This is tubuloglomerular feedback. Low NaCl at the macula densa signals low GFR, so afferent resistance falls and renin release rises, which raises glomerular pressure.

open.q: What response does a fall in NaCl delivery to the macula densa trigger?

questions.q: What is glomerulotubular balance?
options: Reabsorption changes in proportion to GFR, so a constant fraction is reabsorbed
Filtration and reabsorption are equal in every single nephron
Tubular secretion always rises to match any rise in filtration
GFR rises whenever the flow of fluid in the tubule rises
questions.explain: When GFR falls, flow in the tubule slows, giving more time for reabsorption of sodium and chloride. The fraction reabsorbed stays roughly constant, which protects against large changes in sodium excretion.

open.q: What is glomerulotubular balance?

questions.q: Which variables does the Cockcroft-Gault estimate of creatinine clearance use?
options: Age, weight and plasma creatinine, corrected for sex
Body surface area and the haematocrit
Plasma urea, age and plasma sodium
questions.explain: Creatinine clearance = [(140 - age) x weight in kg] / (72 x plasma creatinine in mg/dL), multiplied by 0.85 for women.

open.q: Which variables does the Cockcroft-Gault estimate of creatinine clearance use?

questions.q: Using Cockcroft-Gault, [(140 - age) x weight in kg] / (72 x plasma creatinine in mg/dL), what is the estimated creatinine clearance of a 60-year-old man weighing 72 kg with plasma creatinine 1.0 mg/dL?
questions.explain: (140 - 60) x 72 = 5,760. Divided by 72 x 1.0 = 72, the answer is 80 mL/min. For a woman, multiply the result by 0.85.

open.q: Using Cockcroft-Gault, [(140 - age) x weight in kg] / (72 x plasma creatinine in mg/dL), what is the estimated creatinine clearance of a 60-year-old man weighing 72 kg with plasma creatinine 1.0 mg/dL?

questions.q: Which drug blocks tubular secretion of creatinine, raising plasma creatinine without a true fall in GFR?
questions.explain: Part of the creatinine in urine is secreted by the tubules. Cimetidine (and trimethoprim) block this, so the plasma level rises even though filtration is unchanged.

open.q: Name a drug that blocks tubular secretion of creatinine and raises plasma creatinine without a true fall in GFR.

questions.q: A GFR below which value is end-stage kidney failure, not compatible with long-term life without dialysis or transplant?
questions.explain: In the lecture grading, below 90 is mild, below 60 moderate, below 30 severe and below 15 end-stage kidney failure. Formal CKD staging uses slightly different bands, but 15 is the end-stage cut-off in both.

open.q: A GFR below which value is end-stage kidney failure, not compatible with long-term life without dialysis or transplant?

questions.q: A urine albumin-creatinine ratio above which value suggests kidney damage?
questions.explain: Normally very little albumin is lost in urine. A persistently raised albumin-creatinine ratio (above 30 mg/g, equivalent to about 30 mg/day) is an early sign of kidney disease. The lesser the albumin in urine, the better.

open.q: A urine albumin-creatinine ratio above which value suggests kidney damage?

questions.q: Why is PAH suitable for measuring renal plasma flow?
options: It is filtered only, and none is secreted or reabsorbed
It is broken down inside the kidney, so none reaches urine
It is filtered and then completely reabsorbed by the tubules
It is filtered and secreted, so almost all is removed in one pass
questions.explain: PAH has a high extraction ratio (about 90%) because it is filtered and secreted but not reabsorbed. Its clearance therefore approximates renal plasma flow. It must be measurable in renal artery and vein for the Fick principle.

open.q: Why is PAH suitable for measuring renal plasma flow?

questions.q: Active sodium reabsorption occurs in all tubular segments except which one?
options: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
The descending limb of the loop of Henle
The proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron
The cortical collecting duct of the nephron
questions.explain: The descending limb is permeable to water but not actively transporting sodium. Sodium is actively reabsorbed in the other segments.

open.q: Active sodium reabsorption occurs in all tubular segments except which one?
accept: descending limb of the loop of henle

questions.q: Where is the Na+/K+ ATPase that drives sodium reabsorption located in a tubule cell?
questions.explain: The pump moves sodium out into the interstitium, keeping intracellular sodium low, so sodium flows in from the lumen passively. Water follows by diffusion, so water reabsorption depends on sodium reabsorption.

open.q: Where is the Na+/K+ ATPase that drives sodium reabsorption located in a tubule cell?

questions.q: Which statement about active tubular transport is correct?
options: It always moves down an electrochemical gradient
It saturates, and similar solutes may compete for the carrier
questions.explain: Active transport uses energy (so oxygen is consumed), works against the gradient, saturates at a transport maximum, shows competition between similar molecules and can be poisoned.

open.q: Give two characteristics of active tubular transport.

questions.q: What is the transport maximum (Tm) of a substance?
options: The concentration at which a substance first appears in the blood
The most a substance can be transported per minute; excess appears in urine
The total amount of a substance filtered at the glomerulus each minute
The amount of a substance excreted in the urine each day
questions.explain: Carriers can be saturated. Once the filtered load of glucose exceeds its Tm, the unreabsorbed glucose is excreted.

open.q: What is the transport maximum (Tm) of a substance?

questions.q: Roughly what is the transport maximum for glucose?
questions.explain: The lecture gives 350 mg/min. Textbook values range from about 300 to 375 mg/min, so check which figure your lecturer prefers in exams.

open.q: Roughly what is the transport maximum for glucose?

questions.q: Which substance has a tubular maximum for secretion of about 80 mg/min?
questions.explain: Tm for PAH is about 80 mg/min. Above that, the carrier is saturated, so clearance of PAH falls and it no longer measures renal plasma flow accurately. Inulin is neither secreted nor reabsorbed, so it has no Tm.

open.q: Which substance has a tubular maximum for secretion of about 80 mg/min?

questions.q: How are small proteins and peptides in the filtrate reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
questions.explain: The proximal tubule takes them up into vesicles and breaks them down into amino acids, so almost no protein appears in normal urine.

open.q: How are small proteins and peptides in the filtrate reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?

questions.q: About what fraction of filtered urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
questions.explain: About half is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and the rest enters the loop of Henle, where urea recycling contributes to the medullary gradient.

open.q: About what fraction of filtered urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?

questions.q: Approximately how much glomerular filtrate do both kidneys form each day in a healthy adult?
questions.explain: A GFR of about 125 mL/min gives roughly 180 L of filtrate per day, yet only 1 to 1.5 L is excreted as urine because most is reabsorbed.

open.q: Approximately how much glomerular filtrate do both kidneys form each day in a healthy adult?
accept: Roughly 125 mL per minute over 24 hours

questions.q: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy young adult?
questions.explain: Normal GFR is about 120 to 125 mL/min (roughly 180 L/day) and it falls with age.

open.q: What is the normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy young adult, in mL/min?

questions.q: Which component of plasma is essentially absent from normal glomerular filtrate?
questions.explain: The filtration barrier makes an ultrafiltrate of plasma that is almost protein-free. Small solutes pass freely at the same concentration as in plasma.

open.q: Which major component of plasma is essentially absent from normal glomerular filtrate?

questions.q: Which Starling force in the glomerulus is approximately 18 mmHg and opposes filtration?
questions.explain: Pressure of the fluid in Bowman's space is about 18 mmHg and opposes filtration, as does plasma oncotic pressure of about 32 mmHg. Oncotic pressure in Bowman's space is close to zero because the filtrate has almost no protein.

open.q: Which Starling force in the glomerulus is approximately 18 mmHg and opposes filtration?

questions.q: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is 60 mmHg, Bowman's capsule pressure is 18 mmHg and plasma oncotic pressure is 32 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?
questions.explain: Net filtration pressure is 60 minus 18 minus 32, which is 10 mmHg driving fluid out of the capillary.

open.q: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is 60 mmHg, Bowman's capsule pressure is 18 mmHg and plasma oncotic pressure is 32 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?

questions.q: Clearance of which substance is the gold standard for measuring GFR?
questions.explain: Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed, secreted nor metabolised, so its clearance equals GFR. PAH instead estimates renal plasma flow.

open.q: Which exogenous substance, freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, is the gold standard marker for measuring GFR?

questions.q: Which formula gives the renal clearance of substance X, where U is urine concentration, V is urine flow rate and P is plasma concentration?
questions.explain: Clearance equals urinary excretion rate (U times V) divided by plasma concentration (P). It is the volume of plasma cleared of the substance per minute.

open.q: What is the formula for renal clearance of a substance in terms of urine concentration, urine flow rate and plasma concentration?
accept: Urine concentration times flow divided by plasma concentration

questions.q: What fraction of renal plasma flow is normally filtered at the glomerulus (the filtration fraction)?
questions.explain: Filtration fraction is GFR divided by renal plasma flow, about 125 divided by 625, which is roughly 0.2.

open.q: What fraction of renal plasma flow is normally filtered at the glomerulus?

questions.q: Clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is used to estimate which renal parameter?
questions.explain: PAH is filtered and almost completely secreted, so about 90% is removed in a single pass. Its clearance therefore approximates effective renal plasma flow.

open.q: Clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is used to estimate which renal parameter?

questions.q: Which transporter in the early proximal tubule takes up most of the filtered glucose from the lumen?
questions.explain: SGLT2 is a sodium-glucose cotransporter on the apical membrane of the early proximal tubule. GLUT2 then moves glucose out across the basolateral membrane.

open.q: Which apical sodium-coupled transporter in the early proximal tubule takes up most of the filtered glucose?

questions.q: At approximately what plasma glucose concentration does glucose normally begin to appear in the urine (the renal threshold)?
questions.explain: The renal threshold is about 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL). Above this, some nephrons reach their transport maximum and glucose spills into the urine.

open.q: At approximately what plasma glucose concentration does glucose normally begin to appear in the urine?

questions.q: By what mechanism are filtered amino acids mainly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
questions.explain: Amino acids enter proximal tubule cells by sodium-coupled secondary active transport. Small filtered proteins are the ones taken up by endocytosis.

open.q: By what mechanism are filtered amino acids mainly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?

questions.q: Compared with plasma, tubular fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule is:
questions.explain: Water follows solute through aquaporin-1 and the tight junctions, so proximal reabsorption is iso-osmotic. The fluid volume falls but its osmolality stays the same as plasma.

open.q: Compared with plasma, what is the osmolality of tubular fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule?

questions.q: Which process explains why almost all PAH is removed from the plasma in a single pass through the kidney?
options: Tubular reabsorption in the loop of Henle
Active secretion in the proximal tubule
Passive diffusion in the collecting duct
questions.explain: Filtration removes only about 20% of the PAH reaching the glomerulus. Organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule secrete most of the remainder.

open.q: Which process, in addition to filtration, explains why almost all PAH is removed from the plasma in a single pass through the kidney?

questions.q: About what percentage of filtered water is eventually reabsorbed along the nephron?
questions.explain: Of the roughly 180 L filtered each day, only 1 to 1.5 L is excreted, so about 99% of the filtered water is reabsorbed.

open.q: About what percentage of filtered water is eventually reabsorbed along the nephron?

questions.q: Which nephron segment is virtually impermeable to water, even in the presence of ADH?
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl actively but has no water channels, so the fluid becomes dilute. This is why it is called the diluting segment.

open.q: Which nephron segment is virtually impermeable to water, even in the presence of ADH?

questions.q: Why does plasma oncotic pressure rise along the length of the glomerular capillary?
options: Water leaves while proteins stay behind
Plasma proteins are secreted into the lumen
Red cells are lost into Bowman's space
The capillary wall becomes more permeable
questions.explain: Filtration removes protein-free fluid, so the remaining plasma becomes more concentrated in protein. The oncotic pressure therefore rises and net filtration pressure falls along the capillary.

open.q: Why does plasma oncotic pressure rise along the length of the glomerular capillary?
accept: Protein concentration increases as fluid is filtered

questions.q: What is the effect of constricting the afferent arteriole alone?
options: GFR rises and renal blood flow falls
Both GFR and renal blood flow fall
GFR falls and renal blood flow rises
Both GFR and renal blood flow rise
questions.explain: Afferent constriction raises resistance upstream of the glomerulus, so both blood flow and glomerular capillary pressure fall. GFR therefore falls too.

open.q: What happens to GFR and renal blood flow when the afferent arteriole alone constricts?

questions.q: What is the effect of mild constriction of the efferent arteriole alone?
options: GFR rises and renal blood flow falls
GFR falls and renal blood flow rises
Both GFR and renal blood flow rise
Both GFR and renal blood flow fall
questions.explain: Efferent constriction raises glomerular capillary pressure, so GFR rises. Total flow through the kidney falls because resistance has increased downstream.

open.q: What happens to GFR and renal blood flow when the efferent arteriole alone undergoes mild constriction?
accept: Raised glomerular pressure with reduced flow

questions.q: Efferent arteriolar constriction increases proximal tubular reabsorption mainly because the peritubular capillaries then have:
options: Higher hydrostatic pressure and lower oncotic pressure
Lower hydrostatic pressure and lower oncotic pressure
Higher hydrostatic pressure and higher oncotic pressure
Lower hydrostatic pressure and higher oncotic pressure
questions.explain: Efferent constriction raises the filtration fraction, which concentrates plasma protein, and it lowers pressure downstream. These Starling forces favour uptake of reabsorbed fluid into the peritubular capillaries.

open.q: Why does efferent arteriolar constriction increase fluid reabsorption in the proximal tubule?
accept: Raised peritubular oncotic pressure with lowered hydrostatic pressure
Higher filtration fraction concentrates plasma protein
Starling forces favour uptake in peritubular capillaries

questions.q: If the clearance of a freely filtered substance is greater than the GFR, what does this indicate?
questions.explain: A clearance above GFR means the kidney removes more of the substance than filtration alone can, so the tubules must be adding it by secretion. A clearance below GFR indicates net reabsorption.

open.q: If the clearance of a freely filtered substance is greater than the GFR, what does this indicate about its tubular handling?
accept: Substance added to the filtrate by the tubule

questions.q: Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates true GFR mainly because creatinine is:
options: Partly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
Slightly secreted by the proximal tubule
questions.explain: A small amount of creatinine is secreted by the proximal tubule on top of what is filtered. This overestimate is usually small enough to be accepted clinically.

open.q: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate true GFR?

questions.q: Glomerulotubular balance describes the tendency of the proximal tubule to:
options: Reabsorb a constant fraction of the filtered load
Reabsorb a constant absolute amount regardless of GFR
Secrete more potassium when GFR rises
Stop reabsorbing sodium when GFR rises
questions.explain: Proximal reabsorption rises and falls with GFR so that a roughly constant fraction (about 65%) is reabsorbed. This stops changes in GFR from causing large changes in sodium and water excretion.

open.q: What is glomerulotubular balance?
accept: Constant fractional reabsorption in the proximal tubule

questions.q: A diabetic patient has a plasma glucose of 20 mmol/L and glucose in the urine. Why does glucose appear in the urine?
options: Glucose is secreted by the proximal tubule
The glomerular barrier becomes leaky to glucose
Loop of Henle cannot reabsorb glucose
Filtered load exceeds the transport maximum
questions.explain: The filtered load of glucose exceeds the tubular maximum, so the transporters are saturated and the excess is excreted. This causes an osmotic diuresis and polyuria.

open.q: A diabetic patient has a plasma glucose of 20 mmol/L and glucose in the urine. Why does glucose appear in the urine?

questions.q: A patient with an obstructing ureteric stone has a fall in GFR on that side. Which Starling force has risen to cause this?
questions.explain: Obstruction causes urine to back up and raises pressure in the tubule and Bowman's space. This opposes filtration and reduces net filtration pressure.

open.q: A patient with an obstructing ureteric stone has a fall in GFR on that side. Which Starling force has risen to cause this?

questions.q: After severe haemorrhage a patient's urine output and GFR fall. Which mechanism contributes most to the fall in GFR?
questions.explain: Haemorrhage activates the sympathetic system, which constricts the afferent arteriole and lowers glomerular capillary pressure. Both renal blood flow and GFR fall, conserving volume.

open.q: After severe haemorrhage a patient's urine output and GFR fall. Which change in the glomerular arterioles contributes most to the fall in GFR?

questions.q: A patient's plasma inulin is 0.5 mg/mL, urinary inulin is 30 mg/mL and urine flow is 2 mL/min. What is the GFR?
questions.explain: GFR equals inulin clearance, which is UV divided by P: 30 times 2 divided by 0.5 gives 120 mL/min.

open.q: A patient's plasma inulin is 0.5 mg/mL, urinary inulin is 30 mg/mL and urine flow is 2 mL/min. What is the GFR?

questions.q: Probenecid is sometimes given with penicillin to prolong its action. Which renal process does probenecid inhibit?
options: Reabsorption of penicillin in the loop of Henle
Binding of penicillin to plasma albumin
questions.explain: Penicillin is cleared mainly by secretion through organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule. Probenecid competes for these transporters, so penicillin stays in the plasma for longer.

open.q: Probenecid is sometimes given with penicillin to prolong its action. Which renal process does probenecid inhibit?

questions.q: A child has glycosuria despite a normal plasma glucose, along with amino acids and phosphate in the urine. Which nephron segment is dysfunctional?
questions.explain: Glucose, amino acids and phosphate are all reabsorbed mainly in the proximal tubule. Generalised proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) causes wasting of all of them.

open.q: A child has glycosuria despite a normal plasma glucose, along with amino acids and phosphate in the urine. Which nephron segment is dysfunctional?

questions.q: A patient's PAH clearance is 600 mL/min and the haematocrit is 0.45. What is the approximate renal blood flow?
questions.explain: Renal blood flow equals renal plasma flow divided by (1 minus haematocrit). That is 600 divided by 0.55, which is about 1100 mL/min.

open.q: A patient's PAH clearance is 600 mL/min and the haematocrit is 0.45. What is the approximate renal blood flow?

questions.q: A patient has severe afferent arteriolar constriction. What is the immediate effect on glomerular filtration rate and renal plasma flow?
options: GFR increases while renal plasma flow decreases
GFR decreases while renal plasma flow increases
questions.explain: Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces blood flow into the glomerulus, lowering renal plasma flow and glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, so GFR falls.

open.q: What happens to GFR and renal plasma flow during afferent arteriolar constriction?

questions.q: A patient receives a drug that inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. Which additional effect is expected?
options: Reduced medullary hypertonicity and impaired urine concentration
Increased potassium reabsorption in the collecting duct
Increased water permeability of the thick ascending limb
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Na+, K+ and 2Cl− but is relatively impermeable to water. This contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient; loop diuretics reduce that gradient and impair urine concentration.

open.q: Which nephron segment contains the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter targeted by loop diuretics?
accept: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.q: Which nephron segment normally reabsorbs the largest proportion of filtered sodium and water?
questions.explain: The proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, along with most filtered bicarbonate and nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids under normal conditions.

questions.q: Which property of the thick ascending limb makes it important for generating the renal medullary osmotic gradient?
options: It reabsorbs solute but is relatively impermeable to water
It reabsorbs water more rapidly than sodium
It secretes large quantities of glucose
It is freely permeable to water and urea
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl but is relatively impermeable to water, diluting tubular fluid while adding solute to the medullary interstitium.

questions.q: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus develops glycosuria. Which transport process has reached its capacity?
options: Carrier-mediated glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Glucose filtration across the glomerular basement membrane
Passive glucose diffusion across the loop of Henle
questions.explain: Filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed by sodium-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule. When filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, glucose appears in urine.

questions.q: A drug selectively inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Which immediate tubular effect contributes to its diuretic action?
options: Increased water permeability of the thick ascending limb
questions.explain: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reduces hydrogen-ion generation and bicarbonate reclamation in the proximal tubule, increasing urinary bicarbonate and sodium loss.

questions.q: Which substance is commonly used to estimate glomerular filtration rate because it is freely filtered and is neither significantly reabsorbed nor secreted?
questions.explain: Inulin clearance closely measures GFR because inulin is freely filtered and is not metabolised, reabsorbed or secreted by renal tubules. Creatinine is used clinically as a practical endogenous estimate.
